analysis.one_liner: Bans the use of hydrofluoric acid at oil refineries, requiring a switch to safer refining methods.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in December 2024 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it died without a hearing or a vote as the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: About 40 US oil refineries use hydrofluoric acid to make high-octane gasoline. If released in an accident, natural disaster, or attack, it could kill or permanently injure thousands of people living within 25 miles, and more than 14 million people live near these plants. The bill would have banned hydrofluoric acid at new refineries immediately and at existing ones after five years, forcing a switch to safer, commercially proven alternatives that most refineries already use. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never received any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The more than 14 million people living in the communities surrounding refineries that use hydrofluoric acid, many of them already overburdened by pollution, plus refinery workers exposed on the job. The bill's findings describe a release capable of killing or permanently injuring thousands of people within a 25-mile radius.

how_it_helps.text: Bars new refineries from ever using hydrofluoric acid and gives existing refineries five years to switch to safer refining methods.
Sets a $37,500-per-violation civil penalty and forbids EPA waivers from excusing a refinery from the ban.

Records the danger in its findings: a release could kill or permanently injure thousands of people within a 25-mile radius, and more than 14 million people live in those at-risk communities, many already bearing heavy environmental burdens.

analysis.who_pays: The roughly 40 refineries that use hydrofluoric acid would bear the cost of converting to safer alkylation technology within five years, which could eventually show up in fuel prices.

drawbacks.text: The roughly 40 refineries using hydrofluoric acid would face the cost of converting to alternative technology within five years, a compliance expense that could be passed on in fuel prices.
The bill sets a civil penalty of $37,500 per violation, an amount critics could argue is small relative to refinery revenues and gives operators little financial reason to comply before the deadline.
The bill removes the EPA Administrator's existing waiver authority for this prohibition, so even a refinery that could show a special hardship would have no route to an extension.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is large: eliminating a chemical that could kill or injure thousands of people in an accident or attack, using proven alternatives most refineries already use. The cost side is real but bounded: roughly 40 refineries would have to convert alkylation technology within five years, an expense that could add to gasoline costs. The five-year deadline and $37,500-per-violation penalty were the honest design tradeoffs; critics would say the deadline is tight and the penalty too small to deter a multibillion-dollar operator. On balance, the risk it removes dwarfs the compliance cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in mid-December 2024 and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and the Congress ended three weeks later with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 16, 2024, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
No further action was ever taken; it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill would have amended the Toxic Substances Control Act to bar hydrofluoric acid at refineries, with a five-year deadline for existing plants and a $37,500-per-violation penalty.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The roughly 40 refineries using hydrofluoric acid avoided a mandatory conversion mandate; communities near those refineries remain exposed to the risk the bill targeted.

for.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban hydrofluoric acid at petroleum refineries.

for.name: 10 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Lieu, Barragán, Tlaib, and Norton.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Petroleum refining industry
against.what_they_did: Refining companies have long opposed federal mandates to convert away from hydrofluoric acid, which would require costly retooling of about 40 refineries.

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats sponsored or cosponsored the bill, but with no committee action or vote, the position of most members of either party was never tested.

industries.note: About 40 US refineries would have had five years to replace hydrofluoric acid with commercially proven safer alkylation technology, bearing the conversion cost. The public's protection comes at these companies' expense.
A mandatory refinery conversion would eliminate a specialized industrial customer for the chemical.
